title: New to AI world: How good are 3D modeling AIs?
author: FroyoOk7736
selftext:
Hi everyone \^\^

I wanted to hire some artists to create some 3D custom models for our game... but they cost a lot and cannot afford it

Any suggestions about this topic? I'm afraid that AI 3D models may have some serious issues, especially if they need to be animated (but I may be wrong)

comments.author: Longjumping_Guard726
comments.body:
I've been working as a 3D artist (stylized lowpoly) and I agree, 3D artists are expensive. So I've been offering my clients an option to choose; 
1. I make assets from ground up - expensive but 100% human made
2. I do generate assets - and then I retopo/ reskin and optimize polycounts and materials (usually to a unified single palette texture - since it's my style) - this method is way too cheaper.

I usually use Rodin (hyper 3D) - worked well for me. Also tripo and meshy AI show some good work. But honestly I still believe you can optimize them for your work a lot rather than using the raw AI output.

replies.author: Longjumping_Guard726
replies.body: This: https://youtu.be/43oI7hhF9Xk?si=njqClvX8iGNvlMrQ was built using AI generated assets, but uses a single material across all assets and I reskinned them. I also reduced polycounts a lot by either decimating or quickly building upon the generated model.

replies.author: Melodic-Chemistry127
replies.body: What's the amount of work needed if someone needs to able to swap clothes/armor on the AI generated models? Is that something you would rather do manually from the get go?

replies.author: Longjumping_Guard726
replies.body:
I would like to do it manually because I can do it by myself- I might generate the model first and build on top of that (it's similar to people who sculpt and then retopo on it). 
If you are not familiar with 3D tools like in blender, I suggest you make the meshes separately - body and then cloths etc.

replies.author: FroyoOk7736
replies.body:
And how about an hybrid solution? like, an AI generated base with human tweaks (even major tweaks)  
Would that still be counted as an AI made thing?  
(context: I'm trying to keep my game the more AI free I can, I'M FINE with AI, but audience is not)

replies.author: StickStill9790
replies.body:
The problem is that the audience can’t tell if what you created is AI or not. Plus, in a year, the sentiment will have changed, and the rage trend will be on another topic. Just create your game so that it looks as fantastic as possible.

The problem people have with AI is that it looks unprofessional. Make it polished and no one will care.

replies.author: FroyoOk7736
replies.body:
People seem not to understand that AIs are TOOLS, like an hammer; if we always kept the mindset "if it replaces a human then it's bad", we'd probably still trying to find out how to light a fire

And even if you create only a couple of elements with AI + you heavily edit them, they will not care, it's bad to them and they will dubt about the project being AI slop or asset flip

Devs may understand this, gamers will hardly

replies.author: Longjumping_Guard726
replies.body:
I very well aware of the hate towards AI. I've started my journey pre-AI era, so I know how hard to master something like 3D or understand the concepts of game dev. But I was able to speed up my work in a very efficient way with AI. I've even made free and open source tools that many people use, yet some people comment that they won't use it even though they desperately need it because the code is generated.

I would say nowadays almost any app/ tool in a rush towards bringing AI, you'll see it on Google, social media, news, banking apps, almost anything.. we can't get away from it even though we want it. Same for the games, you think high end studios won't use it under the hood? They will, definitely. We, as indies may not be able to survive without AI in near future. So I'm slowly adapting..

I would say part of the hatred is because people trying to do something 'easily' with AI, just like prompting a whole game - it's bad, you'll probably end up with what they call a slop. But if you know what you doing, how to make (generate) better assets, consistent, how to execute good ideas, I think that's a win. Haters gonna hate but if you can do something outstanding, you'll win.

comments.author: Ignusloki
comments.body:
AI 3d models have improved a lot. I have tested a few local generations and they are ok. They are definitely not up to par to an artist level though. Another thing to keep in mind: 3d model artist usually are already building the model thinking in how to animate it. The 3d AI model won't take that in consideration. So you might have to spend a little more time to tweak the model to work with animation.

My current take: use 3d AI model only for assets that you don't plan to animate.

replies.author: FroyoOk7736
replies.body: Makes sense, I feel animating AI made objects could be quite complex

replies.author: senseven
replies.body: People record themselves running, then ai 'mocaps' that into an animated 3d skeleton. Ai to map that anim to an 3d character. The animator is there for the design and smoothing of the transitions, minus the drudge work.

comments.author: khuzait_haircut
comments.body: Meshy does image to 3d and text to 3d. I only experimented with that service. I'm not advertising for them nor recommending them. I don't have experience with any other tools.

comments.author: Designer_Spell_7270
comments.body: ai 3d models are okay for protos but animations + rigging can get messy. tools like ziva can help but you’ll probably still need to clean stuff manually

comments.author: sumane12
comments.body:
Yeah its good. If you are prepared to edit it and structure your workflows correctly, you can get some incredible results.

The workflow
1) a good reference pic
2) use nano banana or another image editor to split your image into seperate parts, head, arms, hands, body, legs, feet.
3) get multiple angles of each part.
4) generate each part in 3d until you are happy.
5) use the high poly mesh to get normal maps.
6) use a retopo tool (or do it manually) to get a low poly mesh.
7) unless you did it in the previous step, put your model together and optimise for animation, joints etc.
8) use a reskining tool to uv unwrap/paint.
9) rig your model.

comments.author: aostreetart
comments.body: I would say if you want a game optimized model, you still want an artist. AI can make a rough sculpt, it usually has some defects but those tend to snowball into rigging and animation. It's coming along well, but I've been having trouble getting stuff out of it I don't need to cleanup after.

comments.author: Vast_Echo_3004
comments.body:
I do some game dev and 3D prototyping, and my take is that AI 3D tools are useful, but mainly as a starting point.

I still manually clean up and optimize the models before using them in a project, but for quick prototyping, AI tools can be pretty useful.

I’ve been testing Rodin Gen-2.5 recently, and the geometry has been pretty solid. I was able to get a batch of 10 1M-poly models in around 4s, which is helpful when you just want to test ideas quickly.

comments.author: LiveMost4172
comments.body: AI models are getting decent for rough prototyping honestly but animation is usually where the shortcuts start showing up. i found this character model on CGTrader and the difference is pretty obvious once you look at the topology around joints compared to most AI-generated meshes
